sections.heading: Low-frequency and wideband vibration energy harvester with flexible frame and interdigital structure
sections.text:
Pengwei Li,1,a Ying Liu,1,2 Yanfen Wang,1 Cuixian Luo,1 Gang Li,1 Jie Hu,1   
Wei Liu,2 and Wendong Zhang1

1MicroNano System Research Center of College of Information Engineering and Key Lab of Advanced Transducers and Intelligent Control System of the Ministry of Education, Taiyuan University of Technology, Taiyuan 030024, Shanxi, China 2Baicheng Ordnance Test Center of China, Baicheng 137000, Jilin, China

(Received 29 March 2015; accepted 20 April 2015; published online 29 April 2015)

As an alternative to traditional cantilever beam structures and their evolutions, a flexible beam based, interdigital structure, vibration energy harvester has been presented and investigated. The proposed interdigital-shaped oscillator consists of a rectangular flexible frame and series of cantilever beams interdigitally bonded to it. In order to achieve low frequency and wide-bandwidth harvesting, Young’s modulus of materials, frame size and the amount of the cantilevers have been studied systematically. The measured frequency responses of the designed device (PDMS frame, quintuple piezoelectric cantilever beams) show a $460 \%$ increase in bandwidth below $8 0 \mathrm { H z }$ . When excited at an acceleration of $1 . 0 \ \mathrm { g } .$ , the energy harvester achieves to a maximum open-circuit voltage of 65V, and the maximum output power $4 . 5 \mathrm { m W }$ . $©$ 2015 Author(s). sections.heading: I. INTRODUCTION
sections.text:
Recently, integrated circuit, wireless platforms and portable electronic devices are becoming more and more attractive. However, their potential applications in some special environment like wild, biological body, etc. are limited by traditional power supply batteries (big volume, limited life, need to be replaced periodically, and many other unfortunate problems).1–4 Hence, energy harvesting from the environment has been actively explored.5–9 In wide variety kinds of environment energy, ambient mechanical vibrations have been considered as a potential source of power for wireless electronics or sensor applications.10,11 Mechanical-electrical energy conversions based on electromagnetic, electrostatic, and piezoelectric effects have been proposed. Among of which, piezoelectric mechanical vibration energy harvesters have attracted the most attentions, in view of the advantages of high electromechanical coupling and no requirement for external voltage source.12–17

The ambient vibration (e.g. vibration of civil engineering structure and heavy machinery) is always stochastic, intermittent, and mainly distributes in the low frequency $( < 1 0 0 \mathrm { H z } )$ ,18,19 which usually appear as broad peaks rather than sharp ones when reflected in the spectrum. While most of the cantilever’s natural frequencies lie in a narrow frequency range. Should environmental vibration frequency doesn’t match the natural frequency, and then a great drop will occur in output power results.20,21 To maximize the energy harvesting efficiency from the ambient, two kinds of typical methods such as bandwidth widening and working frequency tuning have been developed in previous studies.22–24 Blystad et al. developed a wideband vibration-based energy harvester with a mechanical end stop on one side, an up-sweep bandwidth $9 \ \mathrm { H z }$ (114-123Hz) was measured at $0 . 2 4 \ \mathrm { g }$ acceleration.22 Ferrari designed a piezoelectric multifrequency energy converter using an array of multi-frequency bimorph cantilevers with different natural frequencies, three fundamental resonant frequencies $1 1 3 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ , $1 8 3 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ , and $2 8 1 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ were measured.23 Eichhorn et al. presented a self-tunable piezoelectric generator which was able to self-adjust its resonant frequency between $1 5 0 \ \mathrm { H z }$ and $1 9 0 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ using a microcontroller to perform autonomous frequency tuning.25 However, seldom flexible frame based harvesters for the bandwidth widening researches below $1 0 0 \mathrm { H z }$ have been reported recently.

In this paper, a novel energy harvester structure with low Young’s modulus flexible frame and interdigital structure cantilever beams have been developed. Impacts of the frame dimension and the amount of the cantilever on the system’s resonant frequency have been systematically studied by the finite element analysis method. In the experiment, the realization model of the designed energy harvester with quintuple cantilever beams has been built and investigated.

sections.heading: A. Modeling
sections.text:
Fig. 1(a) shows the conventional piezoelectric energy harvester which consists of a cantilever beam and a proof mass. Until now, this model is widely exploited in many researches.26–29 Unfortunately, such harvester is not suit for the ambient vibration energy harvesting in virtue of its high resonant frequency and narrow operating bandwidth. So, in this article, a novel flexible frame based multi-cantilever beam structure has been designed (Fig. 1(b)-1(d)), which consists of two parts: a frame with low Young’s modulus and a series of cantilever beams. The designed harvester shown as Fig. 1(b) is comprised of the frame and one cantilever beam. Fig. 1(c) and Fig. 1(d) illustrate the vibration-picking structures with triple and quintuple cantilever beams, respectively. Taking the spatial arrangement and stability of the structure into consideration, the cantilever beams bonded to the frame were arranged interdigitally. Fig. 1(e) shows the meshed model of the designed energy harvester with quintuple piezoelectric cantilever beams.

Regardless of the damping and external force, the proposed interdigital-shaped oscillators could be modeled as the mass-spring systems,30 illustrated in Fig 1(b)-1(d). The vibration differential equation is expressed as

$$
M { \ddot { x } } + K x = 0
$$

where $M$ , $\pmb { K }$ and $\boldsymbol { x }$ are the mass matrix, stiffness matrix and displacement of the column vector, respectively. According to the system of differential equations and the model analysis theory, Eq. (1) has the following characteristic solution

$$
x _ { j } = A _ { j } \sin ( \omega t + \theta )
$$

Which shows that when each coordinate of the system deviates from the equilibrium value, the coordinate do simple harmonic motion of different amplitudes at the same frequency of $\omega$ and initial phase angle of $\theta$ . Eq. (2) is written in matrix form as

(d) The designed energy harvester with quintuple piezoelectric cantilever beams, Model D. (e) The finite element mesh of Model D.

$$
x = A \sin ( \omega t + \theta )
$$

Then the Eq. (1) becomes the eigenvalue problem of matrix $\pmb { K }$ and $M$

$$
( K - \lambda M ) A = 0
$$

Where, $\lambda = \omega ^ { 2 }$ . The sufficient and necessary condition for $\pmb { A }$ having nonzero solutions is that λ ωcoefficient determinant equals zero. Thus, we can get Eq. (5), expressed as

$$
( K - \lambda M ) = 0
$$

For the designed energy harvester with single piezoelectric cantilever beam in this paper, where

$$
K = \left| \begin{array} { c c } { { k _ { 1 } + k _ { 2 } } } & { { - k _ { 2 } } } \\ { { - k _ { 2 } } } & { { k _ { 2 } } } \end{array} \right| \quad M = \left| \begin{array} { c c } { { m _ { 1 } } } & { { 0 } } \\ { { 0 } } & { { m _ { 2 } } } \end{array} \right|

According Eq. (5), the system frequency determinant expression would be

$$
\begin{array} { c c } { { \left| k _ { 1 } + k _ { 2 } - \lambda m _ { 1 } \right. } } & { { \left. - k _ { 2 } \right. } } \\ { { \left. - k _ { 2 } \right. } } & { { \left. k _ { 2 } - \lambda m _ { 2 } \right| } } \end{array} = 0
$$

Where, $k _ { 1 } , k _ { 2 }$ represent spring constants of cantilever beam and frame, respectively, $m _ { 1 }$ and $m _ { 2 }$ are the respective effective masses. Thus the Eq. (8) can be drawn as

$$
\lambda ^ { 2 } - \left[ { \frac { k _ { 1 } + k _ { 2 } } { m _ { 1 } } } - { \frac { k _ { 2 } } { m _ { 2 } } } \right] \lambda + { \frac { k _ { 1 } k _ { 2 } } { m _ { 1 } m _ { 2 } } } = 0
$$

Finally, the resonant frequencies $( \omega _ { 1 } ^ { 2 } , \omega _ { 2 } ^ { 2 } )$ of the system can be expressed as

$$
\omega _ { 1 } ^ { 2 } , \omega _ { 2 } ^ { 2 } = \frac { 1 } { 2 } \left\{ \frac { \left( k _ { 1 } + k _ { 2 } \right) m _ { 2 } + k _ { 2 } m _ { 1 } } { m _ { 1 } m _ { 2 } } \right\} \mp \frac { 1 } { 2 } \left[ \left\{ \frac { \left( k _ { 1 } + k _ { 2 } \right) m _ { 2 } + k _ { 2 } m _ { 1 } } { m _ { 1 } m _ { 2 } } \right\} ^ { 2 } - 4 \frac { k _ { 1 } k _ { 2 } } { m _ { 1 } m _ { 2 } } \right] ^ { \frac { 1 } { 2 } }
$$

According to which, it is obviously that the resonant frequencies of the system are directly related to its spring constants $\cdot _ { k } ,$ $\begin{array} { r } { ( k = Y * S / L _ { 0 } , } \end{array}$ Y: Young’s modulus, $s$ : material cross-sectional area, $L _ { 0 }$ : /material original length31) and effective masses $" m '$ . Thus, the resonant frequency of the proposed harvester can be tuned by adjusting the magnitude of the spring constants and effective masses to match well with the vibration of ambient environment.

sections.heading: B. Simulation
sections.text:
A series of analyses have been conducted by the finite element method using COMSOL. In simulation, Piezoelectric Devices Model was utilized; PZT-5H, Cu and iron were selected as the fundamental materials (Table I); and the polarization direction of piezoelectric layers was Z-axis. The bottom and top surfaces were set to be grounded and terminal, respectively, and other surface was zero charge. A linear elastic model was adopted for the non-piezoelectric materials and all the materials were assumed isotropic. Multiple cantilever beams were connected in series. In addition, all the devices were provided by the same excitation with $1 \mathrm { g }$ acceleration at $\mathrm { _ { Z } }$ -axis which was shown in Fig. 1(e), and all the other edges were left free. Finally, resonant frequency and the output voltage were solved via performing the Eigenfrequency Study and Frequency Domain Study, respectively. TABLE I. Fig. 2(a) shows the influence of Young’s modulus of the frame materials (Table II) on the system’s resonant frequency (Model B). The resonant frequency increases exponentially with the Young’s modulus, especially for the second resonant frequency. The simulations demonstrated that the designed energy harvester with a low Young’s modulus frame can shift down the resonant modes to a practical ambient frequency range. Considering the fact that the resonant frequency produced by the special material polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) is lower than other materials, the PDMS was chosen as the frame material. The Poisson’s ratio of the materials was not taken into account in the simulation due to its influence on the resonance frequency is faint.32 The frequency responses of the open-circuit voltage generated by the traditional cantilever energy harvester and the three designed devices were shown in Fig. 3. The traditional cantilever device (line a) has only a single voltage peak (below $8 0 \mathrm { H z } )$ around $6 5 \mathrm { H z }$ with open circuit voltage of $1 3 . 4 4 ~ \mathrm { V / g }$ , whereas the designed device with a single cantilever beam (line b) has two voltage peaks around $1 5 \ \mathrm { H z }$ and $2 3 \ \mathrm { H z }$ with the voltages of $1 7 . 3 7 ~ \mathrm { V / g }$ and $4 . 3 ~ \mathrm { V / g }$ , respectively. The first resonance mode could be assigned to the cantilever beam vibration, while the second resonance mode is from the cantilever beam vibration induced by the frame’s resonance. In addition, the output voltage of the first resonance mode is larger than the traditional device as a result of the greater displacement caused by the flexible frame. TABLE II. The first voltage peak (corresponding to the first resonance mode) arises from the coupled vibration of cantilever 1 and 3. The second voltage peak (corresponding to the second resonance mode) is due to the vibration of cantilever 2. Furthermore, owing to the small frequency spacing between the third and fourth mode, the third voltage peak could be assigned to the combined action of the third and fourth resonance mode which arises from the bending vibrations of cantilevers 1, 3 and cantilever 2, respectively, driven by the frame resonances. The designed device with quintuple cantilever beams (line d) also shows three voltage peaks over the range of $0 { - } 8 0 \ \mathrm { H z }$ , about $7 0 \mathrm { ~ V ~ }$ at $1 2 \ \mathrm { H z }$ , 10V at $2 1 \ \mathrm { H z }$ and $_ { 7 \mathrm { ~ V ~ } }$ at $4 8 \ \mathrm { H z }$ . The first voltage peak can be assigned to the coactions of the first resonance mode (cantilever 2,4 and 5 coupled vibration) and the second resonance mode (cantilever 1, 3 coupled vibration), which results from the small frequency spacing between these two modes. Similarly, the second voltage peak is from the coactions of the third (the bending vibrations of cantilevers 2, 4, 5) and fourth resonance mode (the bending vibrations of cantilevers 1, 3). Moreover, the third voltage peak corresponding to the fifth resonance mode is caused by the vibration of cantilever 2. Comparing with the traditional device, these three proposed structures show much wider bandwidth and lower resonant frequency under $8 0 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ (as shown in Table III). Define the bandwidth as the band between the two frequencies where output voltage amplitude is -3dB of the peak value, so the bandwidth of the traditional device was approximately $5 \ : \mathrm { H z }$ , but for the designed devices with single, triple and quintuple cantilever beams, the bandwidth reach up to $1 1 \ \mathrm { H z }$ , $1 4 \ \mathrm { H z }$ and $2 8 \ \mathrm { H z }$ , exhibiting a $120 \%$ , $180 \%$ and $460 \%$ increase, respectively. The fundamental resonant frequency of the designed devices can be reduced to a quite low level using the low Young’s modulus of the frame. Furthermore, the increase of the number of cantilever beams bonded to the frame results in lower resonant frequency and wider operational bandwidth, which attributes to the equivalent mass growth of the system. Thus, this design concept makes it possible for such devices to be available in practical project applications, such as health monitoring for expressway.

sections.heading: A. Modeling
sections.text:
A prototype with quintuple cantilever beams shown as Fig. 4(a) was devised. This device mainly consists of two parts, a frame of PDMS and a series of cantilever beams which were mounted to the PDMS frame using epoxy bond. The cantilever beam arrays were fabricated with the same PZT, copper cantilever and proof mass for sizes and materials (Table I).

Fig. 4(b) plots the measuring equipment including a function generator (33522A, Agilent), a power amplifier (HEAS-50, Nanjing Foneng Technology Industry Co., Ltd, Nangjing, China), a shaker (HEV-50, Nanjing Foneng Technology Industry Co., Ltd, Nangjing, China), a digital oscilloscope (MSO9104A, Agilent) and a vibration analyzer (XD2006, Sinocera Piezotronics , Inc., Jiangsu, China). The shaker driven by the function generator and the power amplifier was utilized to create a specific harmonic input excitation. The excitation frequency varies from 0 to $1 0 0 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ .

The fabricated device was fixed on the shaker by the fixture; the electricity of every cantilever beam generated was transmitted through two wires which were soldered with upper piezoelectric layer and lower copper layer. Finally, the voltage response generated by the PZT was measured by the digital oscilloscope at a constant acceleration which was monitored using a vibration analyzer.

sections.heading: B. Results and discussions
sections.text:
Fig. 5(a) shows the measured results per base acceleration of the designed energy harvester with quintuple cantilever beams. From this figure, three voltage peaks could be found obviously, about 65V at $1 0 \mathrm { H z }$ , 10.2V at $1 9 \mathrm { H z }$ and $8 . 5 \mathrm { V }$ at 46Hz. These results fit well with the simulation. The errors such as 2Hz frequency shift and 5V output voltage offset, could be attributed to the support conditions of the cantilevered harvester and the measuring system los s.14,33

Fig. 5(b) shows the open circuit voltage and output power measured from the energy harvester with diverse resistive loads at resonant frequency. It could be found that the output voltage increases sharply first $( < 6 0 0 \mathrm { k } \Omega )$ and then slowly with the increased external load resistance. While the output <power increases first, and then decreases with the external load resistance increasing. When the resistive load of $6 0 0 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ was selected, the maximum output power of the designed energy harvester could reach up to $4 . 5 \mathrm { m W }$ at an acceleration of $1 . 0 \mathrm { g }$ .

sections.heading: IV. CONCLUSIONS
sections.text: A flexible beam based interdigital energy harvester for low-frequency and wideband vibration has been developed and tested. The influence factors for the eigenfrequency of the vibration picking system have been studied in detail by adjusting the Young’s modulus, structure, dimension and the amount of the flexible frame and cantilever beams. It was found that the flexible beam with low Young’s modulus was conductive to shifting down the system’s resonant frequency, especially for high-mode of bending motion. In addition, the operational band of the system could be broadened and the resonant frequency would be further reduced, as the amount of the cantilever beam increase. On the basis of finite element analysis, quintuple piezoelectric cantilever beams have been employed and bonded to the PDMS beam in the actual device, which showed lower frequency response and exhibited a $460 \%$ increase in bandwidth compared to the traditional devices. Experiment results show that the designed energy harvester could obtain a maximum output power of $4 . 5 \mathrm { m W }$ at $1 ~ \mathrm { m / s } ^ { 2 }$ acceleration with an optimal resistive load of $6 0 0 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ .
